title: FOT 2025 OPENING: THE EARTHLY AND HEAVENLY TABERNACLES

sense.text: This repeats what verse 14 already said, that he was a partaker of flesh and blood. “For verily he took not on him the nature of angels”: not the nature of angelic, divine beings. “But he took on him the seed of Abraham”: flesh and blood, born of a father and a mother.

“Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren”: in all things he found it suitable to be made like his brethren, flesh and blood.

And this is why: “that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.” He took flesh so he could live and die for the people. Angels don't live and die; they live forever. Christ lived and died for the people.

“For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.” Because Christ took on flesh and blood, he can relate to those covered in flesh and blood. If he were that angel he could not relate, because he would not be in a fleshly form. In a fleshly form he understands us: why we sin, why we go off, the battle we have every day within ourselves. He fought that same battle, but he was not overcome by it.

precepts.why:
Hebrews says it again: “For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.”

Christ was tempted in all points, but at no point in time did he sin. That is why he fasted constantly: to stay in the spirit and to maintain the body he was in.

So he is able to relate to man, because he was tempted like a man, because he was one. That is the high priest of Hebrews 2: one who took on the seed of Abraham and can succour them that are tempted.

sense.text: “As thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee”: this is the tabernacle. The Father dwells in the Son. “That they also may be one in us”: we are all in one accord.

“And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one”: the glory the Father gave the Son, Christ has given to his people, so that they may be one the same way the Father and Son are one.
“I in them, and thou in me”: that goes back to the tabernacle again. Christ dwells in his people as the Father dwells in him, “that they may be made perfect in one.”
“That the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them.” I in them, once again: the tabernacle. Christ dwells in his people.

Regarding the tabernacle: I dwell in them. Peter says “as long as I am in this tabernacle.” What tabernacle? The earthy tabernacle, his body of flesh. While he was still in it, he would “stir you up by putting you in remembrance.”

“Knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle”: I must put this tabernacle off, meaning I am going to die. “Even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me”, because Christ told Peter he would be put to death as an old man.

The point drawn from it is the putting off of this earthly tabernacle. John speaks of the tabernacle, and Peter speaks of it.

“So the Creator of all things gave me a commandment, and he that made me caused my tabernacle to rest”: he that made me is the Father talking to his Son, because Christ is made.

“Let thy dwelling be in Jacob, and thine inheritance in Israel.” The Father is saying, I am going to place you in Israel. You will be that tabernacle; your body will be in Israel. And he conversed with the men of Israel, and the women.
“He created me from the beginning before the world, and I shall never fail.” Christ was created from the beginning, before the world.

“In the holy tabernacle I served before him”: that tabernacle is the one in heaven. “And so was I established in Sion” the same way.

Who dwells in the holy tabernacle? The high priest. So what was Christ in the holy tabernacle in heaven? The high priest. The same position he had in the heavens, he came down and held on the earth: the same exact thing. The heavenly tabernacle and the earthly tabernacle match.

precepts.why:
“This is our God, and there shall none other be accounted of in comparison of him.” No one compares to our God, because only he exists.

“He hath found out all the way of knowledge, and hath given it unto Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved.” So when you read John saying beloved this and beloved that, he is speaking of Israel. We are the beloved. No one else.

“Afterward did he shew himself upon earth, and conversed with men.” Afterward refers to God. He dwelt among men in a body, with a father and a mother. His tabernacle was in Zion. That is how the Father caused Christ's tabernacle to rest, and let his dwelling be in Jacob: his tabernacle was at rest in his people.

sense.text: “But for Adam there was not found an help meet for him.” Adam was still alone. And Adam had that grain of evil seed within him, and he didn't know about it.
“She shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man”: that is what woman means, taken out of man.

“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” They did not know. What does naked mean? It means they were sinful. That grain of evil seed was in them, but they did not know it was there. They didn't know that they were in an earthly tabernacle. That is the point.

precepts.why:
“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.” Hebrews earlier said that Christ is the captain of our salvation through sufferings. He left behind an example of how it is to go through sufferings, affliction, tribulation and persecution. He went first, because when it comes to a king, the king always rides before the army. And the glory shall be revealed within us.

“For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God”: the sons of God are Israel.

“For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly”: that is naked and not ashamed. They did not want it to happen, but that is how they were made, “by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope.”

“Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God.” What is the bondage of corruption? It is that earthy tabernacle that weighs down the soul, the corruptible body the Wisdom of Solomon speaks of in chapter nine.

“For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now”: the whole creation, that is us, groaning and labouring in pain to bring forth. “And not only they, but ourselves also”: not only us, but the world itself, nature itself. Our people being brought to this lower state affects everything, the very nature of things. The world is turned upside down as long as Israel is not ruling the world.
